summary: Shell sort, published by Donald Shell in 1959, generalises insertion sort by first sorting elements that are a large gap apart and then shrinking the gap until it reaches 1. Moving elements long distances early leaves the array almost sorted, so the final gap-1 pass is cheap. Its running time depends entirely on the gap sequence, ranging from O(n^2) for Shell's original sequence to about O(n^(4/3)) for Sedgewick's and Knuth's sequences in practice, in O(1) extra space. It is not stable, but it is short, needs no recursion, and is used in embedded code and in some kernel and library routines.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Insertion sort is fast on nearly sorted data but slow when elements start far from their final positions, because every shift moves an element just one slot. Shell sort attacks that weakness. Pick a **gap** `h`, say 4, and treat the array as `h` interleaved subsequences: indexes 0, 4, 8, ..., then 1, 5, 9, ..., and so on. Insertion-sort each subsequence. An element can now jump `h` positions with one shift, so big-distance disorder is removed quickly. Then repeat with a smaller gap. The array is not yet sorted after a large-gap pass, but it is **h-sorted**, and each smaller pass makes it more nearly sorted. The last pass uses gap 1, which is plain insertion sort, but by then each element is only a few places from home so the pass is close to linear. The key fact, and the reason the algorithm works, is that an array that is h-sorted stays h-sorted after it is k-sorted for another gap k.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: **Gap (increment) `h`**: the distance between elements that are compared and shifted together in one pass.
**Gap sequence**: the decreasing list of gaps, always ending in 1. Choosing it is the whole design problem.
**h-sorted array**: an array where `a[i] <= a[i+h]` for every valid `i`. Each of the `h` interleaved subsequences is sorted.
**Gapped insertion sort**: insertion sort that uses index steps of `h` instead of 1. With `h = 1` it is exactly insertion sort.
**Preservation property**: after you k-sort an h-sorted array it is still h-sorted. That is why later passes do not undo earlier work.
**Not stable**: elements are moved across `h` positions, jumping over equal elements, so equal keys can change their relative order.
**In place**: O(1) extra space, no recursion, no buffers.
**Adaptive**: already-sorted input costs about `n` comparisons per gap, so little more than `n * (number of gaps)` in total.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.body: Sort `[23, 12, 1, 8, 34, 54, 2, 3]` (n = 8) with Shell's gaps n/2, n/4, n/8, that is 4, 2, 1. **Gap 4**: the pairs (index 0, 4), (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 7) are insertion-sorted: 23 and 34 are fine; 12 and 54 are fine; 1 and 2 are fine; 8 and 3 are swapped. The array is now `[23, 12, 1, 3, 34, 54, 2, 8]`. **Gap 2**: the even-index subsequence is 23, 1, 34, 2, which sorts to 1, 2, 23, 34; the odd-index subsequence is 12, 3, 54, 8, which sorts to 3, 8, 12, 54. Interleaved, the array is `[1, 3, 2, 8, 23, 12, 34, 54]`. **Gap 1**: plain insertion sort on this nearly sorted array only fixes two small disorders (3 and 2, then 23 and 12) and ends with `[1, 2, 3, 8, 12, 23, 34, 54]`. The first pass moved 3 forward by four slots in a single shift, which plain insertion sort would take four shifts to do. In the code below, the inner loop is insertion sort with step `gap`: save `a[i]`, shift earlier elements that are `gap` apart and larger, then drop the saved value in the hole.

sections.heading: Variants & Types
bullets: **Shell's original sequence**: `n/2, n/4, ..., 1`. Simple, but the worst case is Theta(n^2), because even and odd positions are not mixed until the last pass (for example when n is a power of 2, large values at even indexes and small values at odd indexes).
**Hibbard**: `2^k - 1`, giving 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, ... Worst case Theta(n^(3/2)). Gaps are consecutive odd numbers that are coprime, so subsequences mix well.
**Knuth**: `(3^k - 1) / 2`, giving 1, 4, 13, 40, 121, ... Use the largest term below `n/3`. Easy to generate (`h = 3h + 1`) and works well in practice, with worst case O(n^(3/2)).
**Sedgewick**: interleaves `9*4^k - 9*2^k + 1` and `4^k - 3*2^k + 1`, giving 1, 5, 19, 41, 109, ... Worst case O(n^(4/3)) and one of the best known practical sequences.
**Pratt**: all numbers of the form `2^p * 3^q` below `n`, giving the provable worst case O(n log^2 n), but many passes make it slower in practice.
**Ciura**: empirically found gaps 1, 4, 10, 23, 57, 132, 301, 701 (extended by `h * 2.25` beyond that). Often the fastest on moderate `n` for random data, though with no proven bound.
**Tokuda**: `ceil((9*(9/4)^k - 4) / 5)`, giving 1, 4, 9, 20, 46, 103, ... Another empirical sequence that performs similarly to Ciura.

sections.heading: Complexity & Costs
bullets: **Space**: O(1). It is in place with no recursion.
**Time, Shell's n/2 gaps**: worst case Theta(n^2); average around O(n^(3/2)) for random data.
**Time, Knuth gaps**: worst case O(n^(3/2)); average behaviour for good sequences falls in the n^1.25 to n^1.5 range quoted for Shell sort generally (exact averages are unproven).
**Time, Sedgewick gaps**: worst case O(n^(4/3)). **Pratt**: O(n log^2 n).
**Lower bound**: no gap sequence is known to give O(n log n) in the worst case, and Poonen showed worst-case Omega(n * (log n / log log n)^2) for any sequence.
**Best case**: sorted data costs about `n` comparisons per gap, so O(n log n) for the n/2 sequence and about `n * (number of gaps)` in general.

**Reference summary**: best case O(n log n) when the data is nearly sorted (depends on the gaps), average case between O(n^1.25) and O(n^1.5) depending on the gap sequence, and worst case O(n^2) for simple sequences such as n/2, n/4, ..., 1. Insertion sort on random data needs about n^2/4 shifts, which is why the gap passes pay off on larger arrays.
**Stability**: not stable. **Number of passes**: about `log2 n` for halving gaps, about `log3 n` for Knuth.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls & Gotchas
bullets: **Forgetting the final gap 1**: without it the array is only h-sorted for the last h, not fully sorted. Every sequence must end in 1.
**Wrong inner-loop bound**: `while (j >= gap && ...)` guards `a[j - gap]`. Writing `j > 0` can read before the array start when `j < gap`.

**Using the shell sequence on adversarial input**: when `n` is a power of two, halving gaps repeatedly compares only even or odd positions together and can degrade to O(n^2). Prefer Knuth, Sedgewick or Ciura gaps.
**Gaps that share factors**: even gaps, such as 8, 4, 2, 1, mean elements at even and odd positions are not compared until the last pass, which wastes the earlier passes.
**Assuming it is stable**: it is not. Sorting by one key after another with Shell sort scrambles the earlier order.
**Integer overflow when generating gaps**: computing `3*h + 1` until it exceeds `n` can overflow a 32-bit `int` for huge `n`. Use `long` or stop early.
**Claiming a clean complexity**: there is no single answer. Always say which gap sequence you mean.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
sections.body: Shell sort suits medium-sized arrays where an O(n log n) algorithm with recursion or buffers is too heavy, embedded systems with little memory, and use as a subroutine in hybrid algorithms. It sits in a useful niche: it is nearly as short to write as insertion sort, needs no recursion or extra memory, and is much faster on medium inputs of thousands to a few hundred thousand elements. It has been used in embedded firmware, in the bzip2 compressor's suffix-sorting step (which uses a Shell-like sort with a Knuth-style increment table), and in the uClibc `qsort` implementation. Its lack of recursion makes it safe where stack space is tiny or must be bounded. For general-purpose use on large data, introsort or Timsort win, so Shell sort is chosen for simplicity and footprint, not for peak speed. It is also a favourite teaching example for algorithm analysis because its complexity depends on number theory.

sections.heading: Interview Notes
bullets: **What is Shell sort in one sentence?** Insertion sort over elements `h` apart for a shrinking `h`, ending with `h = 1`.
**Why does it beat insertion sort?** Early large-gap passes move elements long distances in one step, leaving few inversions for the last pass.
**Complexity?** Depends on gaps: Theta(n^2) for n/2, O(n^(3/2)) for Hibbard and Knuth, O(n^(4/3)) for Sedgewick, O(n log^2 n) for Pratt.
**Is it stable?** No.
**Space?** O(1).
**Best known gaps?** Ciura's for practical sizes, Sedgewick's for a proven bound.
**Why must the last gap be 1?** Only gap 1 guarantees that every adjacent pair is compared, so the array is fully sorted.
**What is an h-sorted array?** One where every subsequence of elements `h` apart is sorted.

subtopics.title: The h-sorting idea
subtopics.summary: Interleaved subsequences and why they help.

sections.body: With gap `h`, indexes split into `h` chains: chain `r` holds `a[r], a[r+h], a[r+2h], ...`. A gapped insertion pass sorts every chain, so the array becomes h-sorted. Think of a 2D grid with `h` columns: h-sorting sorts each column. A large gap means few elements per chain, so each chain sorts quickly, and an element crosses many positions per shift. Because a chain contains a random sample of the whole array's values, it removes the bulk of disorder. Smaller gaps then refine the order using chains with more elements, but by then the elements are already close to their final spot.

subtopics.title: Why later passes keep earlier work

sections.body: A key property makes the algorithm sound: if an array is h-sorted and you then k-sort it, it remains h-sorted. Intuitively, k-sorting only rearranges elements in a way that moves smaller values earlier, and the h-sorted order relation `a[i] <= a[i+h]` survives because each element is moved only past larger ones, in a way that keeps comparable pairs ordered. The consequence is that the work done with the 4-gap is not wasted by the 2-gap pass, and the array becomes progressively more sorted until the final 1-sort completes the job. Proofs use the 0-1 principle or a counting argument on inversions.

subtopics.title: Gap sequences compared
subtopics.summary: How the choice changes the running time.

sections.body: The gap sequence determines the number of passes and how well chains mix. Shell's halving sequence is easy to code but produces gaps that are all powers of two, so for `n` a power of two, elements at odd and even positions are never compared before the last pass, giving the quadratic worst case. Hibbard's `2^k-1` gaps are coprime and give O(n^(3/2)). Knuth's `3h+1` sequence is the easiest good choice: start at 1, repeat `h = 3*h + 1` while `h < n/3`, then walk back down using `h = h / 3`. Sedgewick's has the best proven bound, O(n^(4/3)). Ciura's table of 1, 4, 10, 23, 57, 132, 301, 701 was found by experiment and is the best known for `n` up to a few thousand. For most programs, Knuth or Ciura gives good speed with minimal code.

Take `n = 2^k` and place the `n/2` largest values at even indexes and the `n/2` smallest at odd indexes, each group in sorted order. Every gap except 1 is even, so every earlier pass compares only elements at positions of the same parity: both chains are already sorted and nothing moves. The final gap-1 pass faces an array where every large value at index `2i` must move past about `n/2 - i` small values, which is about `n^2/8` shifts in total. This is why Shell's original sequence is considered poor and why textbooks say to use gaps with no common factors. It is a good interview example because it shows concretely why the gap sequence matters.

subtopics.title: Complexity analysis and open problems
subtopics.summary: What is proven and what is not.

sections.body: Shell sort is unusual because its exact complexity is still not fully known. Knuth gaps are conjectured to be around `O(n^(3/2))` worst case. Sedgewick's sequence has a proven O(n^(4/3)) worst case, and Pratt's has O(n log^2 n). Poonen proved that no gap sequence can achieve better than Omega(n (log n / log log n)^2) worst case, so O(n log n) is impossible for the Shell sort family. Average-case analysis is open for most sequences. For interviews, quote the sequence together with the bound, and mention that practical runs behave like `n^1.25` for good sequences.

subtopics.title: Shell sort versus insertion sort and quick sort

sections.body: Compared with insertion sort, Shell sort wins as soon as `n` passes a few dozen: it reduces total shifts dramatically at the cost of extra loops. Compared with quick sort and merge sort, Shell sort is slower on large inputs (above roughly 100,000 elements) but has no recursion, no extra memory and tiny code, so it wins in constrained environments. Compared with heap sort, it is simpler and often faster on small arrays, but lacks the guaranteed O(n log n) bound. It is not stable, so for sorting records by multiple keys use a stable algorithm. If a question asks for the sort with the best balance of simplicity, in-place operation and decent speed, Shell sort with Knuth or Ciura gaps is a valid answer.

subtopics.title: Comb sort and the shared idea

sections.body: Comb sort applies the same gap idea to bubble sort: compare and swap elements `gap` apart, shrinking the gap by a factor of about 1.3 until it is 1, then finish with bubble passes. Both algorithms remove the 'turtle' problem, where small values near the end move only one slot per pass in simple sorts. Shell sort uses insertion steps and guarantees each pass leaves the array h-sorted; comb sort uses single swaps and needs repeated passes at the final gap. In practice Shell sort with good gaps is faster and more predictable. Both are not stable. The common lesson is that long-distance moves early reduce inversions faster than adjacent moves.

Use a signed index type so `j - gap` comparisons are safe, and keep the guard `j >= gap` before touching `a[j - gap]`. Generate gaps once (a small table such as Ciura's is fastest) and iterate from the largest gap below `n` down to 1. Save `a[i]` in a temporary and write it once at the end of the shifts rather than swapping each time, which reduces writes by about two thirds. If you need stability or a worst-case guarantee, choose a different algorithm. Test with sorted, reversed, all-equal, single-element and empty arrays, and verify the output against a library sort on random data.

subtopics.title: Worked example on nine values
subtopics.summary: Tracing gaps 4, 2 and 1 on a list whose size is not a power of two.

sections.body: Take `[22, 34, 25, 12, 64, 11, 90, 88, 45]` with `n = 9`, so the halving gaps are 4, 2 and 1 (integer division). Gap 4 sorts the chains at indexes (0,4,8) holding 22, 64, 45, which becomes 22, 45, 64; (1,5) holding 34, 11, which becomes 11, 34; and (2,6) and (3,7), which are already ordered. The array is `[22, 11, 25, 12, 45, 34, 90, 88, 64]`. Gap 2 sorts the even-index chain 22, 25, 45, 90, 64 into 22, 25, 45, 64, 90 and the odd-index chain 11, 12, 34, 88 (already sorted), giving `[22, 11, 25, 12, 45, 34, 64, 88, 90]`. Gap 1 is plain insertion sort: 11 moves before 22, 12 shifts past 25 and 22, and 34 shifts past 45, ending with `[11, 12, 22, 25, 34, 45, 64, 88, 90]`. Only a handful of shifts were left for the final pass. Shell sort is often described as the first algorithm to beat O(n^2), which is true for good gap sequences, although the simple halving sequence still has a quadratic worst case.

takeaways: Shell sort runs insertion sort over elements h apart for a decreasing gap sequence that ends in 1.
An h-sorted array stays h-sorted after a smaller k-sort, so later passes never undo earlier progress.
The gap sequence decides the speed: Shell's n/2 is O(n^2) worst case, Knuth and Hibbard O(n^(3/2)), Sedgewick O(n^(4/3)).
It is in place with O(1) space, needs no recursion, and is not stable.
Gaps that share factors (powers of two) leave odd and even positions uncompared until the final pass.
Every sequence must end with gap 1, which makes the final pass an ordinary insertion sort on nearly sorted data.
It is a good choice for medium-size data on constrained systems, but introsort or Timsort win on large inputs.

practice.title: Implement Shell sort with n/2 gaps and print the array after each gap pass for [23, 12, 1, 8, 34, 54, 2, 3].
